stories.headline: Canada and China expand trade pacts and ease tariffs during Carney's visit
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to expand bilateral trade and reduce tariffs, easing Chinese barriers on Canadian pork and seafood in exchange for extended relief on Chinese steel and aluminum. Carney also indicated that Canada could consider Chinese electric vehicle investment if trade negotiations with the United States sour. The bilateral agreements mark a strategic effort by Ottawa to diversify trade partnerships amid growing American protectionism.

stories.headline: Tech firms threaten service pullouts as Ottawa faces pushback on lawful-access bill
stories.summary: Major technology companies including Meta and Signal are urging the federal government to amend its proposed lawful-access legislation, warning they could withdraw encrypted services such as WhatsApp from Canada if compelled to undermine encryption. Legal experts also caution that provisions allowing police to compel metadata retention could face constitutional challenges under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The pressure mounts as civil liberties groups and parliamentary committees examine the potential impact on public digital privacy.

stories.headline: Senior staff leave Pierre Poilievre's office as B.C. Conservatives recruit talent
stories.summary: Five staff members in the office of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, including his deputy chief of staff and senior communications aides, are stepping down from their positions. Multiple departing advisers are moving west to join the newly formed provincial administration of the B.C. Conservatives. The sudden departures create significant personnel gaps in federal strategy and communications ahead of upcoming parliamentary tests.

stories.headline: Canadian inflation remains flat at 3.1 per cent in October
stories.summary: Statistics Canada reported that the national annual inflation rate held steady at 3.1 per cent in October, with gasoline prices persisting as a major upward driver. In light of the flat headline figure, financial economists widely anticipate that the Bank of Canada will keep its key interest rate unchanged at its upcoming December meeting. The inflation data provides monetary policymakers with space to assess economic trends without an immediate need for policy adjustments.

stories.headline: Bank of Canada begins succession planning as Tiff Macklem plans 2027 departure
stories.summary: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem announced that he will not seek a second term when his current seven-year mandate expires on June 2, 2027. The central bank has begun an early search process to evaluate potential internal and external contenders for the leadership post. The transition will determine the future direction of Canadian monetary policy as the bank navigates post-inflation economic challenges.

stories.headline: House of Commons unanimously passes David's Law to expand youth addiction treatment
stories.summary: Members of Parliament voted unanimously to pass David's Law, named in honour of the late son of Conservative MP Luc Berthold who lost his life following struggles with substance use. The legislation shifts federal emphasis toward diversion and treatment programs for youth facing drug dependence before criminal justice sanctions apply. The rare all-party accord reflects shared parliamentary urgency over addressing youth addiction.

stories.headline: Ontario English Catholic teachers vote overwhelmingly in favour of strike mandate
stories.summary: Members of the Ontario English Catholic Teachers' Association voted 98 per cent in favour of a strike mandate across the province, representing 45,000 educators. The union stated the result reflects deep frustration with stalled contract negotiations, while Education Minister Paul Calandra framed the strong mandate as an encouraging sign that teachers want to reach a deal. Formal collective bargaining sessions between the provincial government and the union are set to resume next week.

stories.headline: Ontario medical regulator pauses planned restrictions on safer supply prescribing
stories.summary: The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario has temporarily halted the rollout of new restrictions on safer supply opioid prescribing after being served with a legal challenge. The sweeping regulatory changes, which were scheduled to take effect immediately, sought to impose strict limits on how physicians prescribe pharmaceutical alternatives. The pause leaves current prescribing practices in place while the provincial courts examine the policy.

stories.headline: Roshel to acquire idle Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton
stories.summary: Defence contractor Roshel has reached an agreement to acquire Stellantis's idle auto manufacturing plant in Brampton, Ontario, in order to scale up its armoured vehicle production. Premier Doug Ford demanded that Stellantis ensure laid-off auto workers are rehired to staff future operations at the site. The transaction represents a significant transition of southern Ontario industrial infrastructure toward defence manufacturing amid shifting manufacturing priorities.

stories.headline: Ontario introduces legislation establishing legal process to remove non-consensual intimate images
stories.summary: The Ontario government tabled a new bill on Monday to create an expedited civil legal pathway for victims of intimate image abuse to have non-consensually shared images taken down and deleted. The proposed legislation empowers individuals to pursue direct legal remedies against perpetrators and platforms hosting the material. The measure is designed to provide victims with swifter, less burdensome statutory tools to safeguard personal privacy.

stories.headline: Ontario tables career college OSAP reforms amid funding freeze for students
stories.summary: The provincial government introduced legislation overhauling Ontario Student Assistance Program rules for students attending private career colleges. The legislative reform unfolds against a broader freeze on OSAP disbursements to private colleges, which has left numerous students locked out of classrooms unless they can cover upfront costs privately. Critics and affected learners argue that the new measures do not address the acute financial distress of students currently caught in the funding pause.

stories.headline: Provincial audit attributes Ontario Children's Aid Society costs to complex care needs
stories.summary: A third-party audit commissioned by the Ontario government revealed that rising costs at Children's Aid Societies stem from supporting children with severe, complex needs rather than executive perks or administrative waste. The findings corroborate claims by child welfare advocates that provincial service gaps force agencies into costly emergency arrangements. In response to agency deficits, the government is proceeding with legislation to heighten oversight and financial scrutiny of the sector.

stories.headline: Toronto expands rental development incentives to support up to 10,000 new units
stories.summary: Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow launched the second phase of the city's Purpose-Built Rental Housing Incentives program, offering municipal financial backing to support the construction of up to 10,000 rental units. Under the framework, more than 2,000 of the completed homes will be designated as rent-controlled and affordable. The initiative aims to stimulate rental housing starts and expand workforce housing amidst ongoing municipal affordability pressures.

stories.headline: Peel police charge 12 in multi-million dollar stolen vehicle export bust
stories.summary: Peel Regional Police dismantled a transnational auto theft syndicate, arresting 12 individuals and recovering 96 stolen vehicles valued at approximately $4.5 million. The luxury cars had been loaded into shipping containers bound for export markets in West Africa. The operation underscores ongoing law enforcement efforts across the Greater Toronto Area to disrupt organized vehicle theft networks targeting local communities.

stories.headline: Poll reveals Toronto residents are skeptical of planned Waymo robotaxi rollout
stories.summary: A survey conducted by Liaison Strategies indicates that a majority of Torontonians harbor significant doubts about Waymo's plans to introduce autonomous taxis in the city by 2028. Respondents cited strong apprehensions regarding road safety, interactions with cyclists, and the technology's capability to navigate severe winter conditions. The findings come as testing vehicles continue mapping Toronto streets ahead of prospective commercial deployment.
